summary: This white paper analyzes real-time quantum error correction as a systems engineering problem, proposing a six-layer reference architecture from syndrome acquisition to logical operations and benchmarking major decoders (MWPM, Union-Find, BP+OSD, neural networks) across surface codes and qLDPC codes. The work quantifies the gap between current decoder performance and real-time requirements: MWPM meets the 1 μs per-round deadline for superconducting platforms only at $d \leq 7$ in batch mode, while window-mode decoding is 2–4× more expensive, and GPU-accelerated BP+OSD sustains <1 ms per round for $[\![288,12,18]\!]$ qLDPC codes.
motivation: Quantum error correction has transitioned from algorithmic feasibility to systems engineering challenges following Google's below-threshold surface-code demonstrations, Riverlane/Rigetti's sub-microsecond integrated decoding, and Quantinuum's fault-tolerant logical operations, motivating a systematic analysis of the bottlenecks, latency budgets, and architectural requirements for scalable FTQC.
method: The paper formalizes the end-to-end data path (stabilizer execution, readout, transport, decoding, feedforward), defines streaming versus synchronization regimes with distinct latency requirements, instantiates platform-specific constraints for superconducting ($\lambda \sim 1$ MHz), trapped-ion, and neutral-atom systems, benchmarks decoders under circuit-level depolarizing noise using Stim and PyMatching, and proposes a six-layer stack with heterogeneous compute dispatch, backlog management, and speculative decoding.
result: Batch MWPM achieves $p_{99}$ <1 μs only at $d \leq 5$; window-mode MWPM exceeds 1 μs at all distances. GPU-accelerated BP+OSD for $[\![144,12,12]\!]$ qLDPC sustains 42.5 μs/round at $p=0.001$, meeting 1 ms targets for neutral atoms, while CPU BP+OSD hits 1.04 ms/round at the same code and noise. Speculative decoding, dynamic dispatch, and FPGA/GPU acceleration emerge as essential for scaling to $d \geq 17$ required by practical algorithms like RSA-2048 factoring (~$3.7 \times 10^9$ Toffoli gates).
